canonical_statement: The study tested whether an intravenous heparin dosing nomogram based on body weight achieves therapeutic anticoagulation more rapidly than a standard-care nomogram.

The investigation was a randomized controlled trial conducted simultaneously at two community teaching hospitals: a 700-bed regional referral center in Phoenix, Arizona, and a 250-bed inner-city hospital in Rochester, New York.
Patients were enrolled between May 1991 and January 1992.
During the first 48 hours of anticoagulation, the assigned nomogram determined all heparin dosing decisions and warfarin was withheld.
Eligible patients were admitted for intravenous heparin treatment of pulmonary embolism, proximal deep venous thrombosis, unstable angina, or acute noncoronary arterial ischemia.

Patients were excluded for known allergy to heparin.
A planned total sample size of 100 patients was estimated to provide 90% power at a type I error of 0.05 to detect a 6-hour difference in mean time to the primary outcomes.

The standard-care nomogram used a 5000-unit intravenous bolus followed by 1000 units/hour; for APTT <35 seconds it gave a 5000-unit bolus and increased the infusion by 200 units/hour, for 35-45 seconds a 2500-unit bolus and +100 units/hour, for 46-70 seconds no change, for 71-90 seconds -100 units/hour, and for >90 seconds a 1-hour hold followed by -200 units/hour.

exposures.details: Initial bolus 5000 units; subsequent fixed-unit adjustments based on APTT.

canonical_statement: The weight-based nomogram used actual body weight, with an initial 80 units/kg intravenous bolus followed by 18 units/kg/hour; for APTT <35 seconds it gave an 80 units/kg bolus and +4 units/kg/hour, for 35-45 seconds a 40 units/kg bolus and +2 units/kg/hour, for 46-70 seconds no change, for 71-90 seconds -2 units/kg/hour, and for >90 seconds a 1-hour hold followed by -3 units/kg/hour.

exposures.details: Initial bolus 80 units/kg; subsequent adjustments based on APTT and actual body weight.

canonical_statement: After informed consent, patients were randomized to a nomogram and preprinted orders were charted; staff nurses, who were not blinded, weighed patients, calculated doses, and adjusted infusion rates.
Stat APTT measurements were obtained every 6 hours, and nurses adjusted heparin according to the assigned nomogram when results became available.
No heparin adjustment was made when the APTT specimen had been drawn less than 4 hours after the most recent heparin dose adjustment.
Both hospitals measured APTT using plain Dade actin thromboplastin on automated MLA Electra systems; the normal APTT range at both hospitals was 20 to 30 seconds.
The investigators defined the control APTT as 30 seconds, the upper limit of the hospitals' normal range.
The therapeutic-threshold outcome was elapsed time from heparin initiation until APTT exceeded 45 seconds, corresponding to more than 1.5 times the 30-second control.

outcome.definition: APTT >45 seconds (>1.5 times control)

canonical_statement: The therapeutic-range outcome was elapsed time from heparin initiation until APTT was 46 to 70 seconds, corresponding to 1.5 to 2.3 times control.

canonical_statement: The study therapeutic APTT range of 46 to 70 seconds correlated with anti-factor Xa activity of 0.38 to 0.57 units/mL at the University of Oklahoma Thrombosis and Anticoagulation Laboratory.

Nomogram implementation integrity was assessed using delay from diagnosis to heparin initiation, delay from APTT phlebotomy to dose adjustment, number of APTTs during 48 hours, and the nomogram error rate.
Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia was defined as a decrease in platelet count to less than 100 × 10^9/L.

canonical_statement: Recurrent venous thromboembolism during 3-month follow-up was defined as a new DVT confirmed by venography or Doppler ultrasonography or a new pulmonary embolism confirmed by ventilation-perfusion scanning or pulmonary angiography.

canonical_statement: Blinded researchers reviewed treatment-masked chart portions for in-hospital complications and followed patients treated for venous thromboembolism for 3 months using records and telephone interviews.

Continuous variables were compared with Student t tests and discrete variables with Fisher exact tests; time-to-event outcomes used Kaplan-Meier methods with log-rank tests, and Cox proportional-hazards and logistic-regression models were used for additional analyses.
Among 121 eligible patients, 3 declined and 3 were unable to provide informed consent; 115 patients were randomized.
Of 115 randomized patients, 85 had deep venous thrombosis or pulmonary embolism, 26 had unstable angina, 2 had acute peripheral arterial ischemia, and 2 had crescendo transient ischemic attacks.
Sixty-two patients were randomized to the weight-based nomogram and 53 to the standard-care nomogram.

Baseline characteristics were broadly similar; mean age was 57.6 versus 61.3 years and mean weight was 80.9 versus 76.9 kg in weight-based versus standard care, while bleeding tendency was 8% versus 21% (P=0.06).
Fifteen randomized patients did not remain on protocol for 48 hours, but all were retained in both time-to-event analyses.
Kaplan-Meier analyses favored the weight-based nomogram for both time to exceed the therapeutic threshold and time to enter the therapeutic range (P<0.001 for each).
Mean time to exceed the therapeutic threshold was 8.2 hours with the weight-based nomogram versus 20.2 hours with standard care (P<0.001).

canonical_statement: The authors concluded that the weight-based heparin nomogram was effective, safe, and superior to the studied standard-care nomogram and proposed considering it for adoption as standard practice for hospitalized patients requiring intravenous heparin.

The authors attributed the weight-based nomogram's superior performance primarily to patient-specific dosing by body weight, which placed initial doses closer to eventual heparin requirements and corrected subtherapeutic APTTs more effectively.

Nurses implementing the nomograms were not blinded; the authors argued that they could not influence laboratory APTT measurements and that monitored implementation metrics did not show unintended co-intervention.

The comparison nomogram modeled a prevalent standard of practice rather than an optimized contemporary regimen, and its fixed 1000-unit/hour starting infusion was acknowledged by the authors as insufficient for many patients.
The trial withheld warfarin during the first 48 hours and therefore did not address whether simultaneous warfarin administration changes nomogram performance.

The authors stated that the excess recurrence in standard care could not be attributed solely to initial heparin management because outpatient anticoagulation adequacy was not monitored and two recurrent events occurred after premature warfarin discontinuation.

The authors emphasized that APTT responsiveness depends on reagent and laboratory system; institutions using substantially different assays might need to customize the nomogram's APTT ranges using local calibration or APTT ratios.

The proposed post-study weight-based heparin order sheet used total body weight, repeated PTT 6 hours after each dose change, shifted to daily PTT after two consecutive therapeutic values, and instructed rounding infusion rates to the nearest mL/hour (40 units/hour).
The authors advocated use of the weight-based intravenous heparin nomogram until clearly superior antithrombotic alternatives became widely available.
The study reported grant support from The Palms Clinic, Phoenix, Arizona.
